\section{Integers}
\seclabel{basic-integers}

The trait \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} (\STR{ZZ}) encompasses all finite integers,
the results of starting from \EXP{0} and repeatedly adding or subtracting \EXP{1} a finite number of times.

\Library\ also declare four integer types of fixed size.
The five integer types are these:

\begin{tabbing}
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} (\STR{ZZ}) is the set of integers (it coerces from \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}).
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} (\STR{ZZ64}) is the set of integers representable in 64-bit two's-complement form (it coerces from \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}).
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\STR{ZZ32}) is the set of integers representable in 32-bit two's-complement form.
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{N}64} (\STR{NN64}) is the set of integers representable in 64-bit unsigned binary form (it coerces from \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}).
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} (\STR{NN32}) is the set of integers representable in 32-bit unsigned binary form.
\end{tabbing}

Like every number type, each of them is a subtype of \TYP{Number} and of no other
number type (\secref{basic-rationals}), and each coerces into \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}.
An integer type coerces from each other integer type all of whose values it holds,
as listed above; every other conversion between integer types is written explicitly.

Among the explicit conversions, the method \VAR{narrow} converts a value of
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and a value of
\EXP{\mathbb{N}64} to \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, by keeping its low 32 bits: the result
is the value of the narrower type that is congruent to the argument modulo
\EXP{2^{32}}.
A value that the narrower type holds is unchanged; any other wraps, and no
\TYP{IntegerOverflow} is thrown.

The operators \OPR{LSHIFT} and \OPR{RSHIFT} shift the bits of an integer of any of
the five types by a count of any integer type, and return a value of the type of
the integer shifted.
On \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\VAR{shift}(x,k)} and
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\VAR{shift}(x,-k)}.
On a fixed-size type of width \VAR{n}, for a nonnegative count \VAR{k},
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\lfloor x/2^{k} \rfloor}, and
\EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k} is the value of the type that is congruent to
\EXP{x \cdot 2^{k}} modulo \EXP{2^{n}}: the bits shifted out are lost, and no
\TYP{IntegerOverflow} is thrown.
So a count at or beyond the width gives \EXP{0} for a left shift, and for a right
shift \EXP{0}, or \EXP{-1} if \VAR{x} is negative.
A negative count shifts the other way: \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} (-k)} is
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k}, and \EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} (-k)} is \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k}.
the result of division as \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}}, the power's exponent, the results
of the factorial, of \OPR{CHOOSE} and of the four hyperfloor and hyperceiling
operators as \EXP{\mathbb{N}}, the argument of \OPR{CMP} as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*}, and
the absolute value as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{\geq}}, and it declared twelve check
methods, each returning a refined type or throwing \TYP{CastError}.
The listing and the method entries below extend \TYP{Number} in place of
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*}, declare the coercions from the four
fixed-size integer types, and take \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} or \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} where
the original named a refined type; the check methods leave, since \library\
declare none on the integer types.
The sentences about the infinities of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*} and
\EXP{\mathbb{N}^*} leave the method entries, and so does the sentence that
declared the positive integers a type of their own, ordered by divisibility.
The coercions from the fixed-size integer types are new, with the method entry
that follows.
The exponent of the power, \EXP{\mathbb{N}} in the Working Draft, is now
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, so a negative power is admitted.
The Working Draft gave the result of a negative power through the
exponentiation of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, since \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} was a subtype of
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}: \EXP{2^{-1}} was \EXP{1/2}.
The method entry of the power gives it otherwise: an integer raised to a
negative power is an integer only at the bases \EXP{1} and \EXP{-1}; at a base
of \EXP{0} the power throws \TYP{DivisionByZero}, at any other base it throws
\TYP{IntegerOverflow}, and a fraction is written with a floating-point or
rational base. The method entries of the three unary negations gave the result \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} where the listing gave \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}; on the flat tower that would make the negative of an integer a rational, and they now give \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, as the listing does.}

%%   property FORALL (m, n)  m | n :=: (|\ m/n /| = m/n)
\begin{Fortress}
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{property} \forall (m, n)\;  m \mid n \CONDEQ (\lfloor m/n \rfloor = m/n)\)\-\\\poptabs
\end{Fortress}


%  opr ^(self, power: ZZ): ZZ
\Method{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \mathord{\hbox{\tt\char'136}}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{power}\COLON \mathbb{Z})\COLON \mathbb{Z}}}

Exponentiation of an integer to a nonnegative integer power produces an integer result.
If the \VAR{power} is \EXP{0}, then the result is always \EXP{1}, even if the base is \EXP{0}
(this definition is somewhat arbitrary but is computationally useful).
An integer raised to a negative power is an integer only when the base is
\EXP{1} or \EXP{-1}, and the result is then that exact power, of the base's type.
If the base is \EXP{0}, the power throws \TYP{DivisionByZero}; for any other
base the result is no integer, and the power throws \TYP{IntegerOverflow}.
A fraction is written with a floating-point or rational base: \EXP{2.0^{-1}}
is \EXP{0.5}, and \EXP{(2/3)^{-1}} is \EXP{3/2}.
\revision{revival-integers}{The Working Draft gave this entry no negative power;
its power on \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} gave one, since \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} was a subtype of
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}. The three sentences on a negative power are new.}

%%  property FORALL(x, y:NN) x^y = x^(|\ y/2 /|) x^(|/ y/2 \|)
\begin{Fortress}
{\tt~}\pushtabs\=\+\( \KWD{property} \forall(x, y\COLONOP\mathbb{N})\; x^{y} = x^{(\lfloor y/2 \rfloor)} x^{(\lceil y/2 \rceil)}\)\-\\\poptabs
\end{Fortress}

%%   opr GCD(self, other: ZZ): NN
%%   opr LCM(self, other: ZZ): NN
\Method{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{GCD}}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \mathbb{Z})\COLON \mathbb{Z}}}
\Method*{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{LCM}}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \mathbb{Z})\COLON \mathbb{Z}}}

The operator \OPR{GCD} computes the greatest common divisor of its two arguments.
The result is always nonnegative.  If either argument is \EXP{0}, the result
is the absolute value of the other argument.

The operator \OPR{LCM} computes the least common multiple of its two arguments.
The result is always nonnegative.  If either argument is \EXP{1}, the result
is the absolute value of the other argument.  If either argument is \EXP{0}, the result is \EXP{0}.

The strictly positive integers form a partial order and lattice with
the ``evenly divides'' operator \EXP{\mid} as the partial order operator and
with \OPR{GCD} and \OPR{LCM} as the lattice operators.


%%   property FORALL (m, n) ((m GCD n) | m) AND ((m GCD n) | n)
%%   property FORALL (m, n) (m | (m LCM n)) AND (n | (m LCM n))
%%   property FORALL (m, n) (m GCD n) DOT (m LCM n) = |m DOT n|
\begin{Fortress}
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{property} \forall (m, n)\; ((m \OPR{GCD} n) \mid m) \wedge ((m \OPR{GCD} n) \mid n)\)\\
\(  \KWD{property} \forall (m, n)\; (m \mid (m \OPR{LCM} n)) \wedge (n \mid (m \OPR{LCM} n))\)\\
\(  \KWD{property} \forall (m, n)\; (m \OPR{GCD} n) \cdot (m \OPR{LCM} n) = \left|m \cdot n\right|\)\-\\\poptabs

\subsection{Exponentiation}
Given two expressions \VAR{e} and \EXP{e'} denoting numeric quantities \VAR{v} and \EXP{v'} that
are not vectors or matrices,
the expression \EXP{e^{e'}} denotes the quantity obtained by raising \VAR{v} to the power \EXP{v'}.
This operation is defined in the usual way on numerals.

Given an expression \VAR{e} denoting a vector and an expression \EXP{e'} denoting a value
of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, the expression \EXP{e^{e'}} denotes repeated vector multiplication
of \VAR{e} by itself \EXP{e'} times.

Given an expression \VAR{e} denoting a square matrix and an expression \EXP{e'} denoting a value
of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, the expression \EXP{e^{e'}} denotes repeated matrix multiplication

Underflow is relevant only to floating-point computations and is handled
according to the rules of IEEE 754.

The handling of division by zero depends on the type of the number produced.
For integer results, division by zero throws a \TYP{DivisionByZero}.
For rational results, division by zero produces \EXP{1/0}.
For floating-point results, division by zero produces a \TYP{NaN} value
according to the rules of IEEE 754.
For intervals, division by zero produces an appropriate containing interval
(which under many circumstances will be the interval of all possible real values and infinities).

Multiplication of a vector or matrix by a scalar is done with juxtaposition,
as is multiplication of a vector by a matrix (on either side).  Vector dot product
is expressed by `\EXP{\cdot}' and vector cross product by
`\EXP{\times}'.  Division of
a matrix or vector by a scalar may be expressed using `\EXP{/}'.

The syntactic interaction of juxtaposition, \EXP{\cdot}, \EXP{\times},
and \EXP{/} is subtle.
\See{operator-precedence} for a discussion of the relative precedence of
these operations and how precedence may depend on the use of whitespace.

The handling of overflow depends on the type of the number produced.
For integer results, overflow throws an \TYP{IntegerOverflow}.
Rational computations do not overflow.
For floating-point results, overflow produces \EXP{+\infty} or \EXP{-\infty}
according to the rules of IEEE 754.
For intervals, overflow produces an appropriate containing interval.

This ought to support arbitrary integer types, but right now
    there's no clean way to convert all the arithmetic to use a
    provided type without having an instance of that type in hand.
    Unsigned types in particular are a bit sticky.
 **)
strToInt(s: String, radix: ZZ32): ZZ32 = do
    if |s| = 0 then fail("strToInt of empty string") end
    (i0, neg) =
        if s[0] = '-' then (1, true)
        elif s[0] = '+' then (1, false)
        else (0,false) end
    n = |s| - 1
    r = SUM[\ZZ32\][ i <- i0:n] if d <- digit(s[i], radix) then
                          d radix^(n-i)
                      else
                          fail[\ZZ32\]("strToInt(" s.asString "," radix "): non-digit " s[i].asString)
                      end
    if neg then -r else r end
  end

(** Radix-10 digit conversion.  All caveats of the flexible-radix conversion above apply. *)
strToInt(s: String): ZZ32 = strToInt(s,10)


strToFloat(s: String): RR64 = do   (*) Quick and dirty implementation
  intpart = s.upto('.')
  frac = s.beyond('.')
  both = intpart || frac
  asFloat((SUM[\ZZ32\][k <- 0 # |both|] 10^k (both[|both| - 1 - k].codePoint - '0'.codePoint))/(10^(|frac|)))
end

content.content:
\item[Route C] The same under route~C, which rescues none of the refined types
(\secref{revival-numbers}).
\end{description}

\subsection{The integer trait}
\seclabel{revival-integers}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] \secref{basic-integers}.
\item[Change] The listing of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} extends \TYP{Number} in place of
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*}, keeping its algebra, and declares the
coercions from the four fixed-size integer types, with a method entry for them.
Division returns \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}; the exponent of the power, the results of the
factorial, of \OPR{CHOOSE} and of the four hyperfloor and hyperceiling
operators, the argument of \OPR{CMP}, the absolute value, and the result of
\VAR{lowBits} in its method entry are \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}.
The twelve check methods leave the listing and the method entries. The method entries of the three unary negations give the result \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, as the listing does.
The sentences on the infinities of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}^*}
leave the method entries, and so do the words that made the strictly positive
integers a type extending a lattice trait; the lattice they describe stays.
Another revision gives the result of an integer raised to a negative power in
the method entry of the power: the bases \EXP{1} and \EXP{-1} give their exact
power, a base of \EXP{0} throws \TYP{DivisionByZero}, and any other base throws
\TYP{IntegerOverflow}, since the result is no integer; a fraction is written
with a floating-point or rational base. The box above the listing and a new box
after the method entry say so.
\item[Rationale] \secref{revival-numbers}.
\Library\ declare no infinite integer and no check on the integer types.
Division takes the type the library declares for it; the other signatures take
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, since the library declares none of those methods with a
natural-number type (its power on integers takes an exponent of any integer
type and returns the integer's own type). Route~A gives each number type its own algebra, and the listing's commutative ring over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} negates within \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}; the method entries' \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} held of an integer only while \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} was a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}.
The revision of the negative power follows the revival's decision of
20~October 2026 that each integer type's power answers its own type at every
exponent, raising an error where the result is no integer: the type group's
later code types an integer power by its integer at a signed exponent; no type
carries the sign of an exponent or of a numeral, so that no overloading can give
\EXP{10^{16}} and \EXP{10^{-16}} different types, and the split is on the base,
with the sign tested at run time as \library\ test a sign elsewhere.
Its reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/integer-power-fable-judgement.md}, and its
measurement in \nolinkurl{explorations/perf-probes/integer-power/REPORT.md}, in
the revival's repository.
A reversal to the zero that truncation gives would change only the
interpreter's natives at a negative exponent and the sentences of the method
entry; one to a rational result, typed by the exponent as the Working Draft
typed it, would need the sign of a numeral exponent in its type, which neither
implementation gives.
\item[Effect] As \secref{revival-numbers}.
The integer types no longer hold infinities, so their total order is that of the
finite integers. Negating an integer gives an integer.
The exponent of the power, \EXP{\mathbb{N}} in the Working Draft, is now
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, so a negative power is admitted.
The Working Draft gave the result of a negative power through the
exponentiation of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, since \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} was a subtype of
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}: \EXP{2^{-1}} was \EXP{1/2}
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/numbers.tex}, lines 344--355).
The revised text of \secref{basic-integers} gives it otherwise: \EXP{2^{-1}}
throws \TYP{IntegerOverflow}, and a program that wants \EXP{1/2} writes
\EXP{2.0^{-1}} or a rational base.
The interpreter does so at every integer type, at an exponent of any integer
type, and its integer powers answer the base's own type, as \library\ declare
them; the compiled type checker types them so.
The compiled path's own library does not: its \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} power answers
\EXP{0} at a negative exponent, and a Java exception that no \KWD{catch} sees
at a base of \EXP{0} (rows~441 and~523 of the revival's gap ledger).
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex}:
the listing's lines 196, 239, 246, 249--250, 256, 261, 271--274 and 290--301:
\begin{quote}
\begin{Fortress}
{\tt~~~~}\(    \KWD{extends} \{\, \null\)\(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Z}^*, \TYP{IntegerLike}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}\rrbracket,\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} /(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \mathbb{Z})\COLON \mathbb{Q}^{\#}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} \mathord{\hbox{\tt\char'137}}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{power}\COLON \mathbb{N})\COLON \mathbb{Z}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} (\KWD{self})! \mathrel{\mathtt{:}}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathbb{N}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{CHOOSE}}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \mathbb{Z})\COLON \mathbb{N}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{CMP}}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \mathbb{Z}^*)\COLON \TYP{TotalComparison}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} \left|\mathord{\KWD{self}}\right| \mathrel{\mathtt{:}}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathbb{Z}_{\geq}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} \lhfloor \mathord{\KWD{self}} \rhfloor\COLON \mathbb{N}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} \lhceil \mathord{\KWD{self}} \rhceil\COLON \mathbb{N}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} \lhhfloor \mathord{\KWD{self}} \rhhfloor\COLON \mathbb{N}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} \lhhceil \mathord{\KWD{self}} \rhhceil\COLON \mathbb{N}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \VAR{check}(\KWD{self})\COLON \mathbb{Z} \KWD{throws}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{CastError}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \VAR{check}^*(\KWD{self})\COLON \mathbb{Z}^* \KWD{throws}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{CastError}\)\\

A numeral beside a value of an integer type is converted to that type where no
declaration of the operator is applicable to the two without coercion, and that
type's own declaration of the operator is then the most specific
(\secref{resolving-coercion}); \library\ state on each integer type the
comparisons \EXP{<}, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{>} and \EXP{\geq}, \OPR{CMP},
\OPR{MAXNUM}, \OPR{MINNUM} and a power with a numeral exponent, which the types
inherited before from a declaration that a converted numeral leaves tied with
those of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
Equality and inequality are not converted so: the declaration of \EXP{=} on
\TYP{Number} is applicable to an integer value and a numeral without coercion,
and so is the top-level declaration of \EXP{\neq}, whose parameters are of type
\TYP{Any}; the compiled type checker selects these and converts neither
operand, and \EXP{=} then compares the two as rationals, through the case for a
numeral that this change adds to \VAR{exactValue}, the function by which
\TYP{Number}'s \EXP{=} takes an exact value.
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} states in its api, for the same reason, the additive and
multiplicative operators its body declares.
\TYP{IntLiteral} declares its own \VAR{zero}, \VAR{one}, \VAR{even},
\VAR{odd}, \VAR{floor}, \VAR{ceiling}, \VAR{truncate}, \OPR{DIVIDES},

before as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, since no member of \TYP{Integral} is
applicable to a numeral of that type, even with coercion
(\secref{applicability-with-coercion}).
A numeral given where any integer type is accepted, as the count of a shift,

numeral whose conversions tie.
The interpreter still gives an integer numeral the type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} by its value, so a numeral reaches none

### Forks the batch takes, none consequential

1. **The batch's scope: rungs I and A.** Default: as section 1 gives it. Not consequential: a choice of what is ready, by PLAN's method (the distance's decided sites first) and the planner's probe, reversible in the next batch.
2. **The arrays and decision E's diff: one rung, A.** Default: one rung (section 1). Not consequential: how the work is cut, settled by P-40's "built with the array sites' other fixes" and by the first export error, which clears only with both patches.
3. **The integer power: its own rung, I.** Default: its own rung (section 1). Not consequential: two decisions, two areas, no shared declaration, and the three patches measured applying together.
4. **The array ways as `ways.patch` has them:** the leaf `fill` and `tabulate` for 5 bodies and the `cast` for 9 (1a with 1c), the `cast` in the factory arms (2a), the `cast` of the subscript's value for `Col` and `Row` (3d). Default: as the patch. Not consequential: each is in the ways note's column of ways that need no decision (`reviews/array-sites-ways.md`, section 5), the library's own devices by P-27: a leaf redeclares a parent's method at its own type as `Array1`, `Array2` and `ImmutableArray1` redeclare `copy`, `map`, `ivmap` and `replica`, and the library's `cast` gives a factory's result its sized type, as `array1` and `array2` already do (row 685). The ways not taken, such as 1c alone and 3a's `SubArray2`, are the note's, and the rung's section names those it leaves.
5. **The api's `immutableArray` ranks 2 and 3 put in a comment** (the probe's 4d; `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1500-1501`). The component has had them in a comment since the team's last commit (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2264-2280`; `a874948ac`), and the library has no `ImmutableArray2` or `ImmutableArray3`, so no program can call them. They leave the library chapter of the specification, Part IV, which is the api rendered (`Specification/library/default-libraries.tex:27-37`). Default: as the patch; a point to report, on your review list. Not consequential: the library splits with itself, and the built side wins by the library's own standard, as for `FlatString`'s pair in climb batch 19 (`reviews/batch-19-review.md`, Part 1, split 2); the lines come back by removing the comment.
6. **A guard test of the casts at all eight element types the bound admits.** The ways note measured the casts under walk at four types and the transposed matrix (its section 6, M1), and the other four by reading. Default: A writes a walk test that asserts every cast body's value at `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64`; it passes on the base and after. Not consequential: a cast that fails raises `CastError` where the base answered a value, and the guard shows none does.
7. **`MultiplicativeRing`'s `^` in the api.** The api writes `opr ^(self, other:ZZ64): T`, the component `opr ^(self, other:AnyIntegral): T` with no body (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:283`, `.fss:377`). Three texts, each measured with rung A's patches beside (section 4): (a) `abstract opr ^(self, other:AnyIntegral): T` alone brings a new site, 'The inherited abstract method ^ ... from the trait MultiplicativeRing[\RR64\] has no concrete implementation in the object FloatLiteral in component FortressBuiltin', since `RR64`'s api lacks the component's `opr ^(self, b:AnyIntegral):RR64` (`.fss:486-487`, under the team's comment "Shouldn't need this extra declaration."); (b) the exponent alone, `AnyIntegral`, leaves the entry, which then differs, by reading, only in `abstract`; (c) `abstract` and `AnyIntegral`, with `RR64`'s api declaring the component's `opr ^(self, b:AnyIntegral):RR64`: the entry gone, nothing come. Default: (c). Not consequential: the brief puts this entry with P-153; `abstract` is how the same api trait writes its other bodiless members, `one` and `TIMES` (`.fsi:279-280`); and an api that states its component's declaration is the library's own way.
8. **`QQ`'s api exponent `AnyIntegral`** (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:430`, row 445's api half). Default: in rung I. Not consequential: the row's own fix, the type the component and the specification give.
9. **`QQ`'s body: the `typecase` of the probe's section 4**, the library's device for "any integer" (`exactValue`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:398-408`). Default: as probed, in `power.patch`. Not consequential: P-153's build, as the Fable judgement's section 6 gives it.
10. **`IntLiteral`'s `^` answers `IntLiteral`** (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:552-554`, `.fsi:213-214`), as the probe wrote E. Default: as probed. explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh
#!/bin/bash
# junit.sh <label> <dir-of-tests> <Name.test>... : the gather of climb batch N runs each .test through the
# harness in the main tree (fortress junit, the compiled test harness, as climb batch 6.5's gather ran its pair),
# in the order given, so that a link test runs before its XXX run test. Each named component's cache entries are
# removed before the list and after it. First line: the machine line (protocol.md, principle 2).
# ONE_JVM=1 (added 2026-09-29 for the repair on the merged tree, coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md, "A repair
# of tests and records only"): the whole list in one fortress junit run, one JVM, as the gate's track runs them
# together; Shell junit hands the list to FileTests.suiteFromListOfFiles (Shell.java:1086), which puts its
# compile and link tests before its run tests (FileTests.java:997-1004), so a link test still runs first.
# The environment is env.sh's, set here without sourcing it, since env.sh also removes parser directories in
# /tmp. The tree is the one this script is in. FORTRESS_THREADS=4 is the pin of build.xml's fastTrack macro,
# which runs the gate's compiled tracks. The JVMs keep their temporary files, parser directories among them,
# in the tree's tmp/.
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64
export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH"
export FORTRESS_HOME="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../../.." && pwd)"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
export FORTRESS_THREADS=4
mkdir -p "$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp"
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp"
FH=$FORTRESS_HOME; L=${1:?label}; D=$(cd "${2:?dir}" && pwd); shift 2
cd "$FH/ProjectFortress"
CP=$(../bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
echo "# junit.sh $L $(date -u +%FT%TZ); nproc $(nproc); $(grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //'); $(grep -m1 'cpu MHz' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //') MHz; load at start $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | head -1); FORTRESS_THREADS=$FORTRESS_THREADS; tree $(git -C $FH rev-parse --short HEAD)$(git -C $FH diff --quiet HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library || echo ' with the next rung applied, not yet committed'); tests from $D"
clean () { for t in "$@"; do n=$(sed -n 's/^tests=//p' "$D/$t" | head -1); [ -n "$n" ] && find ../default_repository/caches -name "*$n*" -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null; done; }
clean "$@"
if [ -n "${ONE_JVM:-}" ]; then
  files=(); for t in "$@"; do files+=("$D/$t"); done
  echo "########## [$L] fortress junit, one JVM: $*"
  java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell junit "${files[@]}" 2>&1 | sed "s#$FH/##g" | grep -v '^\s*at ' | cut -c1-240
  echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
else
for t in "$@"; do
  echo "########## [$L] fortress junit $t"
  java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell junit "$D/$t" 2>&1 | sed "s#$FH/##g" | grep -v '^\s*at ' | cut -c1-240
  echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
done
fi
clean "$@"
tests=InferResultOnlyIfWithoutElse
compile
link
run
run_out_contains=PASS

# Rung I (rung-integer-power): the skeptic's verdict

The head judged is `1059606f1`, the worker's last commit. My commits on `wip/rung-integer-power`, in order:

- `1cff513e5`: the worker's `REPORT.md` and `record.md`, written byte for byte from the run's journal by `journal-text.py` (both exited 0).
- `f39076fa8`: a correction of three messages of the walk test (finding 4).
- `4ae8b80ea`: the compiled half of row 441 gets its gated expected-failure test (finding 5).
- `57142f4c9`: corrections of `REPORT.md` and `record.md` (findings 1 to 3, 6 and 7).
- `2f78e98ce`: NEW-I-1's repair measured (finding 8).
- this file.

**Verdict: approved.** The change does what P-153 and the rung's section ask, and the record is honest once corrected. No fix of mine changes code or a decision the worker argued for, and none is contested.

## 1. What I checked

### 1.1 The tables

The worker's head changes no checker code: `git diff --name-only 97ccd5f1f...HEAD` names nothing under `scala_src/` or the checker's generated code. So I read the worker's files and ran no stage. The tables in `REPORT.md` are those of the worker's head (`0bf22171b`'s code, which later commits leave unchanged).

- **Count.** `tmp/rung-integer-power/checker-count-postedit.txt` has '#total 22' and '#locations 22'. Climb batch 19's `climb-batch-19/gate/checker-count.txt` has '#total 28' and '#locations 27'. Every api row is 0, and '#crash none'. The 22 locations in `cc-post/run.txt` are made up of `FortressLibrary.fss:1465`, 19 array sites from `:2528` to `:2979`, and `:4370` and `:4376`. The report said 17 array sites, and 1 + 17 + 2 is not 22 (finding 1).
- **Distance.** `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/compare.sh explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-19/gate/distance.txt tmp/rung-integer-power/distance-postedit.txt` printed:

      DISTANCE DOWN   31 -> 25 (-6)
          kind typecheck               29 -> 23     (-6)
          class GF                      1 -> 0      (-1)  generators: a filter that failed for another reason
          class OT                      9 -> 4      (-5)  other body errors (one-off library slips and checker limits)

  The six sites gone match `explorations/compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv:6-7`, `:10-12` and `:32` (each opened with `awk`). None came. The second export error lost two entries and gained one: MultiplicativeRing's entry is gone, and QQ's entry now names `isNaN` alone. That is 44 entries to 43, read by my own split of the two messages on `(...Decl`. The first export error keeps its 17 entries.
- **Seconds.** The count stage started at 07:34:04 (the transcript's call `5nN12h`), and `stat` of `count-run.txt` gives 07:35:15, so about 71 s. Climb batch 19's gate took about 64 s (the brief). There was no speed pass.

### 1.2 Test first

In the worker's transcript (`agent-a7da6b5cdd4e4c40d.jsonl`), by time and call id:

- 07:14:07 `47Fh1V`: the walk test was written.
- 07:14:24 `nc1eoL`: it ran through the harness on `97ccd5f1f`, with only the test untracked ('?? ProjectFortress/tests/IntegerPowerContractWalk.fss'). It printed 'FAIL: ZZ32 2^(-1) is no integer and throws IntegerOverflow; ...', 'FAILURES!!!' and 'Tests run: 1,  Failures: 1,  Errors: 0'.
- 07:14:40: the three team tests were respelled with `sed`.
- 07:14:52 `owntTy`: the respelled team tests passed on the base, 'OK (3 tests)', with the same 20 printed lines of `compoundArray` as the unchanged file's.
- 07:15:34: `XXXQQPowerExponent` was renamed `QQPowerExponent` (`git mv`).
- 07:15:53 `9RNDor`: `QQPowerExponent` failed on the base: 'Value 3 might not fit in ZZ64.', 'Tests run: 1,  Failures: 1'.
- The first edit of the library or of code came after both failing runs: `git apply` of `power.patch` at 07:17:30 (`ixxg2Y`), the first Java edit at 07:18:11 (`PEgAYp`), and the build at 07:20:39 (`cLn4fE`).
- 07:22:43 to 07:23:06: the test was corrected after the build (the numeral case and the parenthesised `big(…)` bases). At 07:23:27 (`hBaBj2`) the corrected test failed again on the old code, through the base build's harness, with the same FAIL line.
- 07:24:22 `WuHBHM`: the last such run, after the last change of code, printed 'OK (30 tests)' (`h-census.txt:373`).
- `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` followed on that code state: 160, 172, 164 and 169 tests, 0 failures; then 130 tests, 0 failures (`testSystem.txt:769-810`, `testSpecData.txt:188-191`).

The order is as `tests-writing.md`, "The order", gives it: `failureWasRecorded` is true.

### 1.3 The diff, line by line

- **The library.** `git diff 97ccd5f1f -- Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin | diff - explorations/compile-ladder/plan-20/probes/power.patch` printed nothing, so the library change is the planner's patch byte for byte. `git apply --check` of the patch on the base build printed nothing.
- **The natives.** They read as P-153 and fork 11 give them:
  - `Int.Pow`, `Long.Pow`, `NN32.Pow` and `UnsignedLong.Pow` read the exponent by `Int.powCount` and take the negative branch by `Int.negativePow` or `UnsignedLong.negativePow`.
  - `BigNum.Pow` and `IntLiteral.Pow` go through `BigNum.pow`.
  - `powCount` keeps the exponent's sign and parity beyond 64 bits: `Long.MAX_VALUE - 1` is even, `Long.MAX_VALUE` odd, `Long.MIN_VALUE` even and `Long.MIN_VALUE + 1` odd. It treats an `FNN64` of 2^63 or more as positive.
  - `FNN32.getLong` is unsigned (`FNN32.java:31-33`), so an `NN32` exponent is never negative.
  - An `FIntLiteral` exponent can exist only below `Long.MIN_VALUE` (`FIntLiteral.java:40-56`), and it never reaches the `AnyIntegral` overload: `IntLiteral` extends `Number`, not `AnyIntegral`.
  - `powExact` loops at most 63 times at any exponent (`Int.java:402-415`), so 0, 1 and -1 at an exponent beyond 64 bits answer at once.
- **The tests and demos.** The team lines are those of fork 15, a `.0` on each base numeral and nothing else (`git diff` of the six files).
- **The specification.**
  - The method entry's three sentences and the two boxes say what P-153 says.
  - The Appendix I entry gives the change, its reason, the way back, the decision with its date (P-153's commit `d3b5b812d`, 2026-10-20) and the departures with their rows (441, 523).
  - P-96 asks for "a repository document" holding the full reasoning. The entry cites the Fable judgement and the probe's report, as `14e91723f` cited its rung's report.

### 1.4 Precedent

The worker's devices are the library's own:
- the `typecase` over the comprised integer types (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:398-408`);
- `Int.overflow()` (`Int.java:258-261`) for `Int.divisionByZero()`;
- `Int.shiftCount` (`Int.java:295-306`) for `powCount`, with the deviation the report names.

The library also declares `shouldRaise[\Ex extends Exception\](expr: ()->()): ()` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:254`), which `NumberOrderListDeclarations.fss:25-30` uses for `DivisionByZero`. The brief prescribed `PowChooseLcmRungE`'s `overflows` helper and one in its shape, so the worker's `dividesByZero` is the brief's and I left it.

### 1.5 The test's messages

Every citation names a file and a section with an entry, never a line. Three messages say what the cited entry does not say (finding 4). The test has one comment line and is named by its topic.

### 1.6 Programs of my own: the differential

These are under `tmp/rung-integer-power/skeptic/`. They ran under walk with the rung's build (`bin/fortress`, private caches) and with the old code (`old-fortress.sh /home/user/fortress-base20 ... P.fss`), at `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`. The diff shows no mutable variable, field, atomic block or write to a library's state, so there was no four-thread run (the harness runs the gated tests at four).

`SkPowEdgesB.fss` under walk, old | new:

    ZZ32 (-2)^(-1) = -0.5 : RR64|ZZ32 (-2)^(-1) raises IntegerOverflow
    ZZ64 (-1)^(minL) = 1.0 : RR64|ZZ64 (-1)^(minL) = 1 : ZZ64
    NN32 allOnes^(-1) = -1.0 : RR64|NN32 allOnes^(-1) raises IntegerOverflow
    NN64 2^(2^63 NN64) = 1.0 : RR64|NN64 2^(2^63 NN64) raises IntegerOverflow
    QQ (1/2)^(unsigned(3)) raises IntegerOverflow|QQ (1/2)^(unsigned(3)) = 1/8 : QQ

Equal in both: 'ZZ32 2^31 raises IntegerOverflow', 'ZZ32 (-2)^31 = -2147483648 : ZZ32', 'NN32 allOnes^2 raises IntegerOverflow', 'QQ (-2/3)^(-3) = -27/8 : QQ', 'strToInt -45 = -45 : ZZ32', 'strToFloat 1.25 = 1.25 : RR64'.

`SkPowEdges.fss` adds `ZZ` exponents. The old code stops at the first one, 'Value -1 might not fit in ZZ64.'. The new code gives:
- 'ZZ32 (-1)^(big(-1)) = -1 : ZZ32';
- 'ZZ 1^(-big(2)^70) = 1 : ZZ';
- 'QQ (2/3)^(big(-2)) = 9/4 : QQ';
- 'RR64 2.0^(big(3)) = 8.0 : RR64'.

data.summary:
Rung I builds contract E (P-153) correctly, and I approve it with eight corrections. None of them is contested, and none changes code.

The change itself checks out:
- **Library:** it is the planner's power.patch byte for byte (the diff against the patch printed nothing).
- **Walk's six Pow natives:** they read an exponent of any integer type, keeping its sign and parity beyond 64 bits. At a negative exponent 1 and -1 give their exact power, 0 raises DivisionByZero and any other base raises IntegerOverflow.
- **My own walk programs, old code against new:** every value is E's. (-2)^(-1) was -0.5 and now raises; an NN32 or NN64 all-ones base at a negative exponent was -1.0 and now raises; NN64 2^(2^63) was 1.0 and now raises; QQ (1/2)^(unsigned(3)) raised and is now 1/8; ZZ exponents work. The compiled path is unchanged, and old and new print the same lines.
- **Test first:** the transcript shows it. The walk test failed on the base at 07:14:24 and QQPowerExponent at 07:15:53. The patch was applied at 07:17:30 and the build ran at 07:20:39. The test passed after the last code change at 07:24:22 ('OK (30 tests)'), then testSystem passed 665/0 and testSpecData 130/0.
- **Tables:** they match the worker's files. Distance 31 to 25, six sites gone, none come; the second export error goes from 44 entries to 43; count 28 to 22; the count stage took about 71 s.

My corrections:
1. **REPORT.md:** the count has 19 array sites, not 17 (22 = 1 + 19 + 2). The library has 20 fail calls on the base, not 21.
2. **REPORT.md and record.md:** the FACTS text said walk's numeral power answers its own type. It answers a ZZ32 value, which is row 578's defect.
3. **Sentences made false that were not listed:** F-84's "Left: QQ's power (rows 438, 445)", and row 533's claim, which names the api declaration the rung replaced.
4. **IntegerPowerContractWalk.fss:121, :126, :133:** three messages about overflow at a positive exponent now also cite opr-overview.tex's "Multiplication, Division, Modulo, and Remainder Operators" subsection. I re-ran it: it passes on the head and fails on the old code.
5. **Row 441's compiled half gets its home-2 test:** a new expected-failure pair, compiler_tests/XXXIntegerPowerContractCompiled with IntegerPowerContractCompiledLink. Through the harness it shows the expected failure on the old code and on the head, and turns red when the failing part is removed.
6. **NEW-I-2:** it cites FortressLibrary.fsi:1114 on the head, not :1113.
7. **Row 336:** a note for the gather that Int.divisionByZero() now exists.
8. **NEW-I-1's repair is now measured:** with asFloat(t), copies of both BiCGSTAB demos complete (rc 0).

No suite was needed. SKEPTIC.md is committed last, and the branch is pushed.
